content: For individuals with pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) who have no prior history of TB within the last five years or have a remote history of TB treatment (more than five years since treatment completion), the Xpert Ultra test is recommended as the initial diagnostic tool for TB and rifampicin resistance detection in sputum. This is preferred over smear microscopy, culture, and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). This recommendation is strong and supported by high-certainty evidence regarding test accuracy. For adults and adolescents aged 15 years or older with pulmonary TB symptoms and a history of TB treatment completed within the last five years, the Xpert Ultra test may also be used as the initial diagnostic tool for TB and rifampicin resistance detection in sputum, rather than smear microscopy, culture, and phenotypic DST. However, this is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence for test accuracy. In adults and children with symptoms of extrapulmonary TB, the Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra test should be used on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) as the initial diagnostic test for TB meningitis, rather than smear microscopy or culture. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for Xpert MTB/RIF and low-certainty evidence for Xpert Ultra. For extrapulmonary TB in adults and children, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used on lymph node aspirates, lymph node biopsies, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, or urine specimens as the initial diagnostic test for the respective forms of TB, rather than smear microscopy or culture. This is a conditional recommendation with varying levels of evidence certainty depending on the specimen type. In cases of suspected rifampicin resistance in extrapulmonary TB, Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used for resistance detection rather than culture and phenotypic DST. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence for Xpert MTB/RIF and low-certainty evidence for Xpert Ultra. For HIV-positive adults and children with suspected disseminated TB, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used on blood as an initial diagnostic test. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence for test accuracy. In children with pulmonary TB symptoms in settings with a low pretest probability of TB (<5%) and a negative Xpert MTB/RIF result on the initial test, repeated testing with Xpert MTB/RIF on sputum, gastric fluid, nasopharyngeal aspirate, or stool specimens is not recommended. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence for sputum and very low-certainty evidence for other specimen types. In children with pulmonary TB symptoms in settings with a higher pretest probability of TB (≥5%) and a negative Xpert MTB/RIF result on the initial test, a second Xpert MTB/RIF test (for a total of two tests) may be used on sputum, gastric fluid, nasopharyngeal aspirate, or stool specimens. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence for sputum and very low-certainty evidence for other specimen types. For adults in the general population with TB symptoms or chest radiograph abnormalities, Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra may replace culture as the initial test for pulmonary TB. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence for Xpert MTB/RIF and moderate-certainty evidence for Xpert Ultra. The TrueNat MTB or MTB Plus test may be used as an initial diagnostic test for pulmonary TB in children and adults, rather than smear microscopy or culture. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for test accuracy. If TrueNat MTB or MTB Plus yields a positive result, TrueNat MTB-RIF Dx may be used as an initial test for rifampicin resistance detection, rather than culture and phenotypic DST. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence for test accuracy. Moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) may be used on respiratory samples for detecting pulmonary TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, rather than culture and phenotypic DST. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for diagnostic accuracy. The TB-LAMP test may replace sputum-smear microscopy for diagnosing pulmonary TB in adults with TB symptoms. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. TB-LAMP may also be used as a follow-up test to smear microscopy in adults with TB symptoms, especially when further testing of smear-negative specimens is needed. In inpatient settings, the lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assay is strongly recommended to assist in diagnosing TB in HIV-positive adults and children with TB symptoms, advanced HIV disease, or a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³. In outpatient settings, LF-LAM is suggested for HIV-positive individuals with TB symptoms or a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³. However, LF-LAM is not recommended for HIV-positive individuals without TB symptoms or with a CD4 count ≥200 cells/mm³. Low-complexity automated NAATs may be used on sputum for detecting resistance to isoniazid and fluoroquinolones in bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases, rather than culture-based phenotypic DST. For rifampicin-resistant TB, these tests may also detect resistance to ethionamide or amikacin. These are conditional recommendations with varying levels of evidence certainty. Commercial serodiagnostic tests should not be used in children suspected of active pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, regardless of HIV status. This is a strong recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. For children and adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB (without suspicion or evidence of multidrug-resistant TB), a 4-month treatment regimen (2HRZ(E)/2HR) is recommended over the standard 6-month regimen. Non-severe TB includes peripheral lymph node TB, intrathoracic lymph node TB without airway obstruction, uncomplicated TB pleural effusion, or paucibacillary, non-cavitary disease confined to one lung lobe without a miliary pattern. Children with severe TB should receive the standard 6-month regimen or other recommended treatments for severe forms of extrapulmonary TB.
